food.text: Kumis, a fermented drink made from mare's milk, was vital to steppe peoples of Turkic and Mongolic origin, including the Kazakhs, Kalmyks, Kyrgyz, Bashkirs and Mongols, as well as the Yakuts and Siberian Tatars. Because mare's milk contains more sugar than cow's or goat's milk, fermenting it gave kumis a higher, though still mild, alcohol content than kefir.

Because water and fuel were scarce across Central Asia, cooks relied on tandyr ovens fired with poplar wood, saxaul shrubs or dried animal dung to bake flatbread, samsa pastries and meats. Soups, stews and steamed dumplings were instead cooked together in a single cauldron pot.

Nomadic peoples of Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan lived largely on meat and dairy. Besh barmak, a lamb dish eaten with the hands, and horse meat were staples found mainly in Kazakh and Kyrgyz cooking, unlike elsewhere in the region.
The staple grains of Central Asia were millet, rice, wheat and barley. Wheat and rice were ground into flour or cooked whole to make flatbreads such as tandyr nan and noodle dishes like lagman.

Milking a mare for kumis took real skill. The milker knelt on one knee, with a pail propped on the other knee, one arm wrapped behind the mare's rear leg and the other in front, while a foal was allowed to start the milk flowing before being pulled away.

A Central Asian meal was traditionally laid out on a floor cloth called a dastarkhan. It opened with tea or tandyr-baked bread, continued with a soup called shorpo or pulled noodles called lagman, and reached a main course of pilov, a rice dish with meat and carrots.

Tea was the most popular drink across Central Asia, drunk green with cream in Kyrgyz households and black among Kazakhs and Uzbeks. People gathered to drink it socially in a dedicated teahouse called a chaikhana.

In Mongolia, mares were traditionally milked for kumis only between mid-June and early October. During that season a single mare could produce roughly 1,000 to 1,200 litres of milk, about half of which was left for her foal.

Kumis itself was only mildly alcoholic, at 0.7 to 2.5 percent. Central Asian nomads nonetheless found ways to strengthen it, such as freeze distillation, or to turn it into a stronger distilled drink called arkhi.

Pilov, Central Asia's most iconic dish of rice cooked with meat and carrots, had countless regional variations. Uzbek cooks in particular added raisins, dried apricots, nuts or legumes to enrich the basic recipe.

art.text: In Bukhara, the Shaybanids created the present Po-i-Kalyan complex and integrated the Qarakhanid-era Kalan Minaret into it. They renovated the old mosque in 1514 and added the large Mir-i 'Arab Madrasa in 1535-6.
In Samarkand, the local ruler Yalangtush Bi Alchin gave the Registan its current appearance. He built two new madrasas across from the Ulugh Beg Madrasa.

After Mongolia was conquered by the Manchu dynasty, Mongol style bows were officially outlawed. Manchu soldiers entered gers and broke any Mongol bows they found, and the Qing forced Mongols to use the Manchu bow. Over two hundred years, the ancient art of Mongol bow making was nearly lost.

In 1576 the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism became the state religion of Mongolia. Monks were some of the leading intellectuals in Mongolia, responsible for much of the literature and art of the pre-modern period.
The Sherdar Madrasa in Samarkand's Registan (1616-1636) imitates the form of the Ulugh Beg Madrasa. The Tilakari Madrasa (1646-1660) is both a mosque and a madrasa.
Architectural activity became less significant in Central Asia after the 17th century. The exception was Khiva, the center of the Khanate of Khiva.

From the 17th century onward, most traditional bows in Mongolia were replaced with the similar Manchu bow. It is mainly distinguished by larger siyahs and prominent string bridges. Modern Mongolian bows derive from this Chinese and Manchu tradition.

Zanabazar (1635-1723) and Zaya Pandita (1599-1662) are counted among the most famous Mongol holy men. They belonged to a Gelug monastic world whose monks produced much of Mongolia's literature and art before the modern period.

The Po-i-Kalyan mosque in Bukhara follows the traditional layout: a large rectangular courtyard surrounded by four iwans, with prayer halls covered by domes on pillars. The maqsura is covered by a large double-shelled dome on a tall cylindrical drum. The mosque is built of brick, decorated with both tilework and brickwork.

The Friday mosque of Khiva has a distinctive hypostyle hall of wooden columns and was rebuilt in this form in 1788-9. It stands in Itchan Kala, the inner fortified section of the city, along with some of Khiva's other historic Islamic-era monuments.

war.text: For millennia the horse archers of the steppe were some of the most militarily potent people in the world. Their dominance ended in the 16th century, when firearms allowed settled people to gain control of the region. The Russian Empire and the Qing dynasty of China then expanded into Central Asia.

The Dzungars were the last steppe empire to emerge, and they conquered much of East Turkestan and Mongolia. In a sign of the changed times, they could not match the Chinese and were decisively defeated by Qing forces. The Qianlong Emperor took control of Xinjiang in 1758.

During the 18th century, Kazakh raids on Russia's territory of Orenburg were common. The Kazakhs captured many Russians and sold them as slaves in the Central Asian market. In 1717, 3,000 Russian slaves, men, women and children, were sold in Khiva by Kazakh and Kyrgyz tribesmen.

Under Peter the Great there was a major Russian push southeast, alongside the expeditions up the Irtysh River. It included the disastrous 1717 attempt to conquer Khiva, in which the Russian force split into five groups after the khan's offer of peace and was massacred, and Cherkassky and his retinue were beheaded in front of the khan.

In 1715, Colonel Bukhholts went up the Irtysh River with 3,000 men and began building a fort at Lake Yamysh. The site was on the fringe of the Dzungar Khanate, and the Dzungars drove them off. The Russians retreated downriver and founded Omsk.

In 1713, reports reached Peter the Great that gold had been discovered in Yarkand, deep in the Dzungar Khanate. A large expedition sent the following year to build a fort line toward the region was almost completely wiped out by the Dzungars through siege by 1716.

In the 1750s two descendants of Afaq Khoja, the brothers Burhan al-Din and Khwaja-i Jahan, were held hostage by the Dzungars at Ili, then aided the Qing in a campaign to annihilate the Dzungars. From spring 1755 to summer 1757 the 300,000-strong Qing army massacred around 300,000 Dzungars regardless of gender and age, under orders to liquidate the whole Dzungar nation down to the last baby, and survivors were killed by a smallpox epidemic. The total loss of population in Dzungaria reached 1,000,000, leaving it a land without people. In 1755 Khwaja Jahan, carrying out Burhan al-Din's order, razed to the ground the Golden and Silver temples in Ghulja and Kainuk in the Ili River Valley, which Galdan Boshugtu Khan had built as sacred symbols of Dzungar power.

In 1714, Alexander Bekovich-Cherkassky was sent to the Khanate of Khiva, ostensibly to celebrate the accession of Shergazi Khan. His real aim was to find Yarkand and learn whether a river connected it to the Caspian Sea. He reported that a river existed, but that a Khivan dam had redirected it from the Caspian to the Aral Sea.

In 1720, Ivan Likharev went up the Irtysh River and founded Ust-Kamenogorsk. The Dzungars, who had just been weakened by the Chinese, left the Russians alone this time. Several other places were built on the Irtysh at about the same time.

In 1722, over 5,000 Russian prisoners were in Bukhara. Raiders had stolen cattle, robbed Russian villages and trapped people in captivity, then sold them in the slave markets of Central Asia. In 1730, Kazakh raids into Russian lands were a constant irritant and led to the enslavement of many of the Tsar's subjects, who were sold on the Kazakh steppe.

In summer 1774, Russian troops in the Kazan region were busy suppressing the rebellion led by the Cossack leader Pugachev. The Kazakhs took advantage and launched more than 240 raids along the Orenburg border. They captured many Russians and herds.

Contemporary depictions of the 1768 Battle of Khorgos between the Qing dynasty and the Western Mongolian Dzungars show the mounted Dzungars mostly armed with muskets, not bows. This reflects how firearms had displaced horseback archery in the region.

In 1736, urged on by Kirilov, the Kazakhs of the Lesser and Middle Hordes launched raids into Bashkir lands, killing or capturing many Bashkirs in the Siberian and Nogay districts. In 1755, Nepliuev tried to win Kazakh support by promising that the Kazakhs could keep the Bashkir women and children living among them. Thousands of Bashkirs would be massacred or taken captive by Kazakhs over the course of the uprising.
Raiding on the Russian frontier continued to the very end of the 18th century. In 1799, the biggest Russian caravan plundered in that period lost goods worth 295,000 rubles.

literature.text: In 1648, the Oirat Buddhist monk Zaya Pandita created the Clear Script, a new alphabet for the Oirat language based on the traditional Mongolian script. It resolved ambiguities in the older script by adding symbols for vowels and vowel lengths, and it made it easier to transcribe Sanskrit and the Tibetic languages.

The Kyrgyz Epic of Manas, though tradition holds it to be far older, describes historical events that historians place in the 16th and 17th centuries. The earliest written reference to its hero Manas and his enemy Joloy appears in a Persian manuscript dated 1792.

In 1587, the translator and scholar Ayuush Güüsh created the Galik alphabet, inspired by the third Dalai Lama, Sonam Gyatso. It added extra characters to the traditional Mongolian script so that Tibetan and Sanskrit terms could be transcribed when translating religious texts.

Classical Mongolian, a highly standardized written language quite distinct from the vernacular that followed it, began developing in the 17th century. Its most notable works from this period include the Mongolian Kangyur and Tengyur, the translated Buddhist canon, along with several chronicles.

Starting in the late 16th century, Tibetan Buddhism gained a foothold among the Mongols, and rising literacy led to a new Altan Tobchi by an unknown author in the 1620s. It combined the earlier parts of the Secret History with the older apocryphal legend cycle.

Zaya Pandita, born in 1599 to a minor Khoshut prince, traveled to Lhasa in 1615 to study Buddhism before becoming a missionary among the Oirat and Khalkha Mongols. After creating the Clear Script in 1648, he spent until his death in 1662 translating about 186 Buddhist texts from Tibetan into the Oirat language.

The scholar Hatto argued that the Epic of Manas was compiled to glorify Sufi sheikhs of Shirkent and Kasan, and that circumstances make it highly probable the epic is a late 18th century interpolation. This view runs against Kyrgyz tradition, which holds the epic to be much older than that.

In 1686, the Soyombo alphabet was created specifically for writing Buddhist texts in Mongolian. It offers distinctive evidence of the phonological peculiarities of early Classical Mongolian at the time.

The 17th century Mongolian chronicle Altan Tobchi, or 'Golden Chronicle,' was written by Lubsang-Danzin and preserves about two-thirds of the Secret History of the Mongols in a slightly different version. It joined other works, such as the Jami' al-tawarikh, that had also drawn on the older text.

Divan poetry, collections of poems by a single author, reached its strongest period between the 16th and 18th centuries with a balance of Persian and Turkish elements. Poets such as the Uyghur Ali-Shir Nava'i (1441-1501) had argued for the status of the Turkic languages. In the early 19th century, however, Persian influence began to predominate again.

In 1651 the monk Lubsang-Danzin expanded the Altan Tobchi narrative, now usually called the Lu Altan Tobchi, and included a full two-thirds of the Secret History. This version was discovered in 1926 by Duke Jamiyan from Dornod.

The Clear Script was mainly used by the Oirat and neighboring Mongols in the late 17th and early 18th centuries, chiefly to translate Buddhist works from Tibetan. Surviving informal letters from the late 1690s show it was also used for everyday writing, not just for religious texts.

Mongolian scribes traditionally wrote with a reed pen until the 18th century, when the brush replaced it under Chinese influence. Ink, either black or cinnabar red, was applied to materials such as birch bark, paper, and cloth made of silk or cotton.

After the fall of the Ming dynasty and the rise of the Qing dynasty, Chinese transcriptions of the Secret History of the Mongols began to be copied and disseminated more widely. These transcriptions preserved the Mongolian pronunciation as it had been rendered into Chinese characters at the Hanlin Academy.

science.text: According to Mongolian tradition, in 1745 a Buddhist disciple made several unsuccessful attempts to fly using a device he had invented that was similar to a parachute. It stands as one of the era's most unusual homegrown invention stories from the steppe.

Despite resistance from Siberian tribes, Russian Cossacks pushed from the Urals all the way to the Pacific Ocean in just 57 years, between 1582 and 1639. They did it by threading together short portages linking rivers that ran roughly east to west.

Siberia's three great rivers, the Ob, the Yenisey and the Lena, all flow north into the Arctic Ocean, so explorers linked them with short portages to travel east and west across the flat terrain. Furs were shipped along this river network because they were far easier to move by water than over land.

The would-be aviator was Bunia, a Buddhist disciple connected to Erdene Zuu Monastery in Kharkhorin, Övörkhangai Province. Built in 1585, it is considered Mongolia's earliest surviving Buddhist monastery.

One well-traveled route ran from Tobolsk, near the capital of the conquered Khanate of Sibir, down the Irtysh to the Ob River, then up the Ob and the Ket River. From there, a portage reached the Yenisei River at Yeniseysk, founded in 1619.

The Tobol River, the main tributary of the Irtysh in Western Siberia, was one of the four important rivers of the Siberia Khanate. In 1428 the khan was killed in a battle with the forces of Abu'l-Khayr Khan at the Battle of Tobol. In the 16th century the Tobol was the eastern terminus of a portage route leading west to the Vishera and Kama rivers.

Before roads reached Siberia in the 1730s, travel depended entirely on rivers and portages like these. One route ran from Mangazeya, founded in 1601 on the Taz River, toward the Yenisei and eventually the Lena River at Yakutsk.

politics.text: The long dominance of the steppe nomads ended in the 16th century, when firearms allowed settled people to gain control of the region. The Russian Empire, the Qing dynasty of China and other powers then expanded into the area. By the end of the 19th century they had seized the bulk of Central Asia.

Between 1582 and 1639, Cossack adventurers made themselves masters of the Siberian forests. They did not expand south, because they were seeking furs. They knew little of the steppe, and the steppe nomads were numerous and warlike.

By 1507, Uzbeks under Shaybani Khan had conquered almost all of the surviving Timurid principalities, including Samarkand and Herat. This ended the rule of the Timurid dynasty's smaller states in Central Asia and Khorasan.

The Kazakh Khanate was left weak after the death of Tauke Khan in 1715, and central authority passed to its three clan confederations, the jüzes. Facing raids and pressure from the Russian Empire, they sought Russian protection. In 1730, Abū'l-Khair Khan, Khan of the Junior jüz, sent an envoy formally requesting subjugation to Russia.

After the fall of the Yuan dynasty in 1368, the Genghisid rulers retreated to the Mongolian Plateau. They continued to rule there until 1635, when they surrendered to the Later Jin dynasty, which later evolved into the Qing dynasty. This rump state is known as the Northern Yuan.

The Mongol Eight Banners were formally established in 1635 by Hong Taiji of the Later Jin dynasty, which was renamed the Qing dynasty the following year. At their founding, about 10,000 warriors were incorporated. Some Mongols, like the Kharchin in 1622, joined the Jurchens through formal sworn alliances.

Babur, a Timurid prince, was exiled from Fergana after repeated conflicts with Shaybani Khan. In 1504 he established a new base at Kabul, which had previously been under the rule of his uncle Ulugh Beg II. From Kabul he invaded the declining Delhi Sultanate in 1526.

Alexey Ivanovich Tevkelev met the leaders of the Junior jüz on 10 October 1731 and officially incorporated the region into the Russian Empire. On December 15, 1731, emissaries were sent to Semeke Khan of the Middle jüz, who accepted and gave his oath of allegiance. Empress Anna confirmed the Senior jüz's admission in 1738.

By the year 1800, Chinese Inner Asia consisted of four regions: Manchuria, Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang. Many had only recently been conquered by the Qing dynasty and were governed through different structures from the older Chinese provinces. A Qing agency, the Lifan Yuan, supervised them.

After the Yuan dynasty fell in 1368, the Yuan remnants who retreated to Mongolia kept using the title "Great Yuan". Certain Mongol leaders still evoked the name on occasion up to the early 17th century, long after the dynasty's fall.

Membership in a Mongol Eight Banner was hereditary and followed the patrilineal line. The Mongol banners were the smallest of the three ethnic divisions, at about 8% of all bannermen. An estimated 100,000 to 200,000 men and women were enrolled in 1648, with the population roughly doubling by 1720.

philosophy.text: Zaya Pandita Namkhaijamts (1599–1662) was an Oirat Buddhist scholar who studied in Lhasa under the Panchen Lama before returning to spread Tibetan Buddhism among the Mongols. Between 1648 and his death in 1662 he translated roughly 186 Buddhist texts from Tibetan into Oirat.

In 1585 Abtai Sain Khan, ruler of the Khalkha Mongols, ordered the construction of Erdene Zuu monastery after meeting the 3rd Dalai Lama, when Tibetan Buddhism was declared the state religion of Mongolia. Builders used stones taken from the ruins of Karakorum, the thirteenth-century Mongol capital, to construct the new monastery.

Afaq Khoja was a Naqshbandi Sufi leader who held the title of Khwaja and ruled as a political leader in Kashgaria, in present-day southern Xinjiang. In 1691 he swore to "exterminate all descendants of Chengiz Khan" after Muhammad Imin Khan expelled him from Yarkent, and in 1692 his army defeated Muhammad Imin Khan, who fled to the mountains where he was captured and killed. Afaq Khoja died in 1694 and left his son Yahiya Khoja as ruler of the Yarkand Khanate; Yahiya Khoja was then killed by Afaq Khoja's wife Khanam Padshah, a daughter of Sultan Said Baba Khan.

In 1678 the Oirat leader Galdan received the title of Boshogtu Khan from the Dalai Lama, a religious honor that made the Dzungars the leading tribe among the Oirats. Dzungar rulers themselves, however, used the separate title of Khong Tayiji, meaning crown prince, rather than khan.

To spread Buddhist teaching among the Oirats, Zaya Pandita created a new alphabet called the Clear Script, or Todo bichig, in 1648, adapting the traditional Mongolian alphabet to remove ambiguities in pronunciation. The script let him translate Buddhist scripture directly into the Oirat language.

In 1640 the Buddhist teacher Zaya Pandita helped the Oirat leader Erdeni Batur convene a pan-Mongol conference between the Oirat and the Khalkha Mongols. The conference aimed to unite the two peoples against outside enemies and to settle their internal disputes peacefully rather than through war.

Zaya Pandita was born the fifth son of Babakhan, a minor Khoshut prince who had converted to Tibetan Buddhism and wished one of his sons to join the Buddhist clergy. In 1615 Zaya traveled to Lhasa as a novice monk to study Buddhism, including under the guidance of the 4th Panchen Lama.

Erdene Zuu monastery was damaged in 1688 during one of the many wars fought between the Dzungars and the Khalkha Mongols. After the fighting the monastery was abandoned, and local people dismantled its wooden fortifications for their own use.

In 1638 the Panchen Lama directed Zaya Pandita to leave Tibet and carry out missionary work among the Mongols. He went on to spread Tibetan Buddhism not only among the Oirat and Khalkha Mongols but also to the Kalmyk people who had settled far away in Russia.

culture.text: In 1576 the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism became the state religion of Mongolia. Shamanism was absorbed into the state religion while being marginalized in its purer forms, later surviving only in far northern Mongolia. The general populace nevertheless still practised Shamanism.

After the Mongol Empire broke up, the Mongols retreated to form the Northern Yuan, and a cult of worship formed around the image of Genghis Khan as a supernatural being. This came amid a decline in literacy. Chronicles such as the Chinggis Qaan-u Altan Tobchi replaced the semi-historical narrative of the Secret History with an apocryphal image of the Khan.

Zanabazar (1635-1723) and Zaya Pandita (1599-1662) are among the most famous Mongol holy men. The 4th Dalai Lama, Yonten Gyatso (1589-1617), was a Mongol himself and is recognized as the only non-Tibetan Dalai Lama.

The word Dalai is a combination of the Mongolian word dalai, meaning "ocean", and the Tibetan word bla-ma, meaning "guru, teacher, mentor". The title thus joins two languages, and the 4th Dalai Lama, Yonten Gyatso, was a Mongol.

The Mongol Eight Banners were divided by color: Plain and Bordered Yellow, White, Blue and Red. Each was initially subordinate to the chiefs of the Manchu banner of the same color. Some Mongols, like the Kharchin in 1622, joined the Jurchens in large numbers through formal sworn alliances.
